docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This block diagram is for my specific module for Team 301's project. My module is part of the drive train that will move our robot. The circuity will require specific voltage levels, such as 3.3V for the logic of the ESP32 and the logic for the motor driver, and 12V to power the motor. I will be using a 12V DC motor to drive half of the drive train of our robot. I will use a motor driver to control the motor and allow it to move forwards and backwards. We will be connecting to each other with UART and GPIO pins. It will be powered by a 12V 2A AC/DC power supply that will connect to a 3.3V switching power regulator.

docs.title: Table 1: Motor Driver
docs.text:
Component Pros Cons -Choice 3 -12-V, 1.76-A BRUSHED DC MOTOR DR -Texas Instruments -Link -Datasheet -Cheapest -Protection features -Has CAD file -Only for DC brushed motors -Under 12V -Choice 1 -IFX9201SGAUMA1 - Infineon Technologies $3.55/each -Link -Datasheet -Used in class before -Has CAD model -Has High Voltage and Current Intake -No reverse polarity protection -Current has wide tolerance -Choice 2 -IC BRUSHED MOTOR DRVR 8TSSOP -Toshiba Semiconductor and Storage -$0.83/each -Link -Datasheet -Inexpensive -High Voltage & Current intake -Has CAD file -Only for DC brushed motors -Sensitive thermal conditions

Rationale: Choice 2. We have used this motor driver in class and know how it works. It works with 12V and 3.3V logic. Choice 3 is a close second but it does not have SPI.

docs.title: Table 2: DC Motor
docs.text:
Component Pros Cons -Choice 1 -STANDARD MOTOR 6600 RPM 12V -SparkFun Electronics -$2.75/each -Link -Datasheet -Cheap -Can intake 12V -2-wire setup -Low torque -Needs a custom footprint -Little data on the datasheet -Choice 2 -GEARMOTOR 35 RPM 12V MICRO METAL -Pololu $37.95 -Link -Datasheet -Uses 12V -High torque -2-wire connection -High power -Needs a custom footprint -May be too slow -Choice 3 -GEARMOTOR 220 RPM 12V MICR METAL -Pololu -$26.45 -Link -Datasheet -Steady speed -2-wire connection -Uses 12V -Might be not enough torque/not fast enough -May not be suitable for a drive train -Needs a custom footprint

Rationale: Choice 3. This motor has a good amount of speed and torque, and uses 12V. It should be able to run our drive train well.

docs.title: Table 3: 3.3V 1.5A Switching Power Supply
docs.text:
Component Pros Cons -Choice 1 -LM2575-3.3WU-TR -onsemi -$2.16/each -Link -Datasheet -Inexpensive -Have used in class before -Wide input voltage range -Lower switching frequency -Larger footprint -Choice 2 -LM2575D2T-3.3R4G -Microchip Technology -$1.75/each -Link -Datasheet -Cheapest -High switching frequency -Low output current -Requires a feedforward capacitor for high voltages -Choice 3 -LM2594MX-3.3/NOPB -Texas Instruments -$3.97/each -Link -Datasheet -Broad operating temperature range -Lower thermal resistance -Expensive -More pins, bigger component -Lower switching frequency

Rationale: Choice 1. We have used this voltage regulator before, so I know how to wire and use it. Choice 2 was close, however it has a low max current output, making choice 1 the best voltage regulator to pick.

docs.title: Table 4: 12V 2A AC-DC Wall Power Supply
docs.text:
Component Pros Cons -Choice 1 L6R24-120 -Tri-Mag, LLC -$10.38/each -Link -Datasheet -Inexpensive -Has less noise Average Efficiency -The cord is short -Choice 2 -WSU120-2000 -Triad Magnetics -$15.07 each -Link -Datasheet -Average Efficiency -Inexpensive -More Expensive -Has more noise -Choice 3 MDS-030AAC12 AB -Delta Electronics -$29.26/each -Link -Datasheet -Medical Power Supply -Average Efficiency -Very Expensive -Big

Rationale: Choice 1. This power supply has low output noise and is not too expensive. The other power supplies are around the same, but choice 2 has more noise, and choice 3 is overkill, as it is for medical devices.

docs.text: B - Bryce H - Hattie T - Tim F - Riley W - Rylee E - Everyone

docs.title: API – Motor Driver (Node 0x02)
docs.text: Owner: Bryce (B) Subsystem: Motor Driver Node ID: 0x02 Protocol: Team 301 (Big-endian)

docs.title: 0x0001 — Set Motor Speed
docs.text:
From: Riley (F) or upstream To: Bryce (B) Type: Receive

Command to set motor speed and direction.

Byte(s) Field Type Bytes Min Max Example 4–5 message_type uint16_t 2 0x0001 0x0001 0x0001 6 motor_id uint8_t 1 1 5 1 7 speed_high uint8_t 1 0 255 0 8 speed_low uint8_t 1 0 255 150 9 direction uint8_t 1 0 1 0 10 control_flags uint8_t 1 0 255 0 11–61 reserved uint8_t[] 51 0 0 0x00…

Notes - Speed = (speed_high << 8) | speed_low - Valid RPM: 0–1000 - control_flags undefined (team spec gap)

docs.title: 0x0002 — Request Telemetry
docs.text:
From: Riley (F) To: Everyone (E) Type: Receive (Broadcast)

Requests telemetry data from all nodes.

Byte(s) Field Type Bytes Min Max Example 4–5 message_type uint16_t 2 0x0002 0x0002 0x0002 6 telemetry_mask uint8_t 1 0 255 0x1F 7 timeout_sec uint8_t 1 1 255 5 8–61 reserved uint8_t[] 54 0 0 0x00…

Notes - bit4 = Motor RPM - Only responds if bit4 is set

docs.title: 0x0003 — Telemetry Packet
docs.text:
From: Bryce (B) To: Riley (F) Type: Send

Telemetry response containing motor status.

Byte(s) Field Type Bytes Min Max Example 4–5 message_type uint16_t 2 0x0003 0x0003 6–7 distance_mm uint16_t 2 0 0 8 motion uint8_t 1 0 1 9–10 temperature_tenths_c int16_t 2 0 0 11–12 motor_rpm uint16_t 2 0 1000 300 13 status_flags uint8_t 1 0 7 14–61 reserved uint8_t[] 48 0 0

Notes - bit0 = running - bit1 = error - bit2 = low battery

docs.title: 0x0004 — ACK
docs.text:
From: Bryce (B) To: Original sender Type: Send

Acknowledges successful command execution.

Byte(s) Field Type Bytes Min Max 4–5 message_type uint16_t 2 0x0004 0x0004 6 acked_msg_type uint8_t 1 0x01 0xFF 7 status uint8_t 1 0 1 8 error_code uint8_t 1 0 0x08 9–61 text char[] 53 — —

docs.title: 0x0005 — Error / Event Log
docs.text:
From: Bryce (B) To: Riley (F) Type: Send

Sent when a motor fault occurs.

Byte(s) Field Type Bytes Min Max Example 4–5 message_type uint16_t 2 0x0005 0x0005 6 error_code uint8_t 1 0x01 0x08 0x03 7 severity uint8_t 1 0 3 2 8–61 message_text char[] 54 — —

Error Codes 0x01 Motor not found 0x02 Invalid parameter 0x03 Overcurrent 0x04 TTL expired 0x05 Destination unreachable 0x06 CRC failure 0x07 Unsupported message 0x08 Resource busy

Table 1: Example component selection

External Clock Module

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. XC1259TR-ND surface mount crystal$1/eachlink to product * Inexpensive[^1]* Compatible with PSoC* Meets surface mount constraint of project * Requires external components and support circuitry for interface* Needs special PCB layout. * Option 2. * CTX936TR-ND surface mount oscillator * $1/each * Link to product * Outputs a square wave * Stable over operating temperature * Direct interface with PSoC (no external circuitry required) range * More expensive * Slow shipping speed

Choice: Option 2: CTX936TR-ND surface mount oscillator

Rationale: A clock oscillator is easier to work with because it requires no external circuitry in order to interface with the PSoC. This is particularly important because we are not sure of the electrical characteristics of the PCB, which could affect the oscillation of a crystal. While the shipping speed is slow, according to the website if we order this week it will arrive within 3 weeks.
